chief_complaint: chronic inflammatory lower back pain and morning stiffness improving with exercise
hpi_details: 29M presenting with a 6-month history of chronic low back pain worst at night and in the early morning, improving with exercise, associated with Achilles enthesitis and a past episode of anterior uveitis.
ideas: He thinks he severely strained his lower back from bad posture at his desk job and lifting weights at the gym.
concerns: He is worried that his worsening morning stiffness will make him unable to keep up with his full-time job and that he might need spine surgery.
expectations: He hopes to get stronger pain medication or muscle relaxants and a referral for physical therapy so he can get through his workday.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Ankylosing Spondylitis (Axial Spondyloarthritis) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Ankylosing Spondylitis (Axial Spondyloarthritis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes confirmatory HLA-B27/imaging workup followed by NSAID first-line therapy with escalation to biologics, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chronic inflammatory lower back pain and morning stiffness improving with exercise

Key HPI features: 29M presenting with a 6-month history of chronic low back pain worst at night and in the early morning, improving with exercise, associated with Achilles enthesitis and a past episode of anterior uveitis.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Reduced lumbar flexion (positive Schober test), reduced chest expansion, tenderness over the SI joints (positive FABER/Gaenslen tests), and tenderness at the Achilles insertion (enthesitis). No active eye inflammation on exam today. Normal peripheral joint exam, no synovitis.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Ankylosing Spondylitis (Axial Spondyloarthritis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Mechanical low back pain without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Eye pain and redness — could indicate acute anterior uveitis, a treatable extra-articular manifestation.
management_principles: Diagnose per ASAS criteria: sacroiliac imaging (radiograph, or MRI with STIR sequences if radiographs are normal but suspicion remains high) plus clinical features, or HLA-B27 plus multiple additional spondyloarthritis features
First-line pharmacologic treatment is NSAIDs; escalate to biologic therapy (TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor) if there is inadequate response after an adequate trial
Emphasize physical therapy and a structured exercise program to maintain spinal mobility and function
Screen for and urgently refer any acute anterior uveitis (painful red eye, photophobia) to ophthalmology.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 29M presenting with a 6-month history of chronic low back pain worst at night and in the early morning, improving with exercise, associated with Achilles enthesitis and a past episode of anterior uveitis.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Reduced lumbar flexion (positive Schober test), reduced chest expansion, tenderness over the SI joints (positive FABER/Gaenslen tests), and tenderness at the Achilles insertion. No active eye inflammation on exam today. Normal peripheral joint exam, no synovitis.
reference_soap.assessment: Chronic inflammatory back pain with enthesitis and a history of uveitis, clinically consistent with axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis); confirmatory HLA-B27 testing and sacroiliac imaging are pending.
reference_soap.plan: Order HLA-B27 testing, sacroiliac joint imaging, and inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) to support the diagnosis per ASAS criteria. Refer to rheumatology for NSAID first-line therapy with escalation to a TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor if inadequate response. Emphasize physical therapy and an exercise program, and instruct the patient to seek urgent ophthalmology review for any future acute red-eye symptoms.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Ankylosing Spondylitis Axial Spondyloarthritis
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for chronic inflammatory lower back pain and morning stiffness improving with exercise
Select appropriate confirmatory testing (HLA-B27, sacroiliac imaging) per ASAS classification criteria for suspected axial spondyloarthritis
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: An HLA-B27-associated inflammatory arthritis of the spine and sacroiliac joints causing chronic low back pain worse at night and in the morning, improving with exercise — the opposite pattern from mechanical back pain.
red_flags: Eye pain and redness — could indicate acute anterior uveitis, a treatable extra-articular manifestation

must_ask.say: Is your back pain worse at night and in the morning, and does exercise help?
How long has this back pain been going on?
Have you had pain at the back of your heel, like your Achilles tendon?
Have you ever had a painful red eye?
Does anyone in your family have similar back problems or arthritis?

history.answer: My lower back has been aching and feeling terribly stiff for months, especially when I wake up in the morning.
The pain is deep in my lower back and upper buttocks on both sides. It does not shoot down into my legs or feet.
It started slowly about six months ago without any injury, fall, or heavy lifting.
It feels like a deep, persistent ache that is usually around a 5 out of 10.
Sitting still or lying down makes it worse, but walking around and doing light exercises actually helps. Coughing or sneezing doesn't change it.
Yes, I often wake up during the second half of the night because my back aches, and resting in bed does not relieve it.
My back is very stiff every morning for about an hour or more until I shower and get moving.
No, I haven't noticed any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my legs.
No, I have no numbness around my private parts and no trouble controlling my bladder or bowels.
Walking actually helps my back loosen up, and my legs don't feel heavy or painful when I walk.
No, I haven't had any fevers, chills, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss.
No, I have never had cancer.
No, I have not had any recent infections, spinal injections, or procedures, and I do not use intravenous drugs.
No, I have never taken steroids long-term and have no history of weak bones or fractures.
No, I have no stomach pain, no pulsing sensation in my belly, and no burning or blood in my urine.
Yes, the back of my left heel has been quite sore and tender where the cord attaches, particularly when I take my first steps.
About a year ago my right eye became painfully red and light-sensitive, and the eye doctor told me it was uveitis. It went away with eye drops and is fine now.
No, I don't have any flaky skin patches, scalp rash, or long-standing diarrhea.
I took over-the-counter ibuprofen a couple of times and it helped a lot, but I don't take it regularly.
I work full-time as an accountant, so I sit at a desk for long stretches, which makes me feel stiffer.
Waking up in pain every night has been exhausting and frustrating, and it leaves me tired during the day.

I thought I just pulled something really badly at the gym or messed up my back from slouching at my desk all day. I'm terrified that this stiffness will get so bad I won't be able to sit through my shifts at work or that I might end up needing spinal surgery.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or kidney disease.
I have never had surgery and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any regular medications, vitamins, or supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications or anything else.
I have never smoked. I only drink socially, having one or two beers on the weekend with friends.
I live in an apartment with my partner, and our building has an elevator.
My uncle has severe back stiffness and arthritis, but neither of my parents has spinal conditions.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Normal visual acuity and pupillary light reflexes, with no conjunctival injection, ciliary flush, or active intraocular inflammation.
Chest expansion is reduced at 2.0 cm measured at the fourth intercostal space; no chest wall tenderness.
Normal spinal curvature; tenderness elicited over bilateral sacroiliac joints, restricted lumbar forward flexion on modified Schober test (12 cm), and negative straight leg raise bilaterally.
Tenderness at the left Achilles tendon insertion and positive FABER test bilaterally; no peripheral joint swelling, effusion, or warmth.
Motor strength is 5/5 across all major muscle groups in bilateral lower extremities.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation throughout the L1-S1 dermatomes bilaterally.
Patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally with downgoing plantar responses.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, with no palpable pulsatile aortic mass or organomegaly.
No psoriatic plaques, nail pitting, or rashes observed.
